title: Is there a pharmacy near here?
title_target: Il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
goal: Say that something exists, describe where things are, and ask about places nearby.
bekal: use *il y a* and its negative *il n'y a pas de*
say where things are: *sur, sous, dans, devant, derrière, à côté de*
merge *de* with the article: *du, de la, des*
wave: Go back to **Unit 8** first: tell the story of your own day from getting up to going to bed, using *d'abord, ensuite, après, enfin*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Dans le quartier
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved into a new room and asks his neighbor about the area.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Excusez-moi, il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
lines.id: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?
lines.literal: excuse-me, it there has a pharmacy near from-here?

lines.speaker: Voisine:
lines.text: Oui, il y en a une au bout de la rue.
lines.id: Yes, there's one at the end of the street.
lines.literal: yes, it there of-it has one at-the end of the street.

lines.speaker: Voisine:
lines.text: Juste en face de la pharmacie. Elle est excellente.
lines.id: Right across from the pharmacy. It's excellent.
lines.literal: just in face of the pharmacy. she is excellent.

lines.speaker: Voisine:
lines.text: Il y a un petit magasin à côté de la banque.
lines.id: There's a small store next to the bank.
lines.literal: it there has a small store at side of the bank.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Il n'y a pas de grand supermarché dans le quartier ?
lines.id: Isn't there a big supermarket in the neighborhood?
lines.literal: it not-there has not of big supermarket in the neighborhood?

lines.speaker: Voisine:
lines.text: Non, mais il y en a un derrière la gare.
lines.id: No, but there's one behind the train station.
lines.literal: no, but it there of-it has one behind the station.

lines.speaker: Voisine:
lines.text: Non, à dix minutes à pied. Vous avez un plan ?
lines.id: No, ten minutes on foot. Do you have a map?
lines.literal: no, at ten minutes on foot. you have a map?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Non, mais j'ai mon téléphone. Merci beaucoup !
lines.id: No, but I have my phone. Thanks a lot!
lines.literal: no, but I-have my phone. thanks much!

lines.speaker: Voisine:
lines.text: Je vous en prie. Bienvenue dans le quartier !
lines.id: You're welcome. Welcome to the neighborhood!
lines.literal: I you of-it pray. welcome in the neighborhood!

notes: **Il y a means both "there is" and "there are".** *Il y a une pharmacie*, *il y a trois pharmacies* — the form never changes. English distinguishes *there is* from *there are*; French doesn't bother.

**The negative drops the article.** *Il y a un supermarché* → *il n'y a pas **de** supermarché*. The old rule from Units 4 and 6 is back — and it will keep coming back until you don't have to think about it.

**Il y en a un** = "there's one (of them)". The little word *en* stands for the thing already mentioned, so you don't have to repeat it. You don't need to produce it yourself at A1, but you'll hear it constantly, so learn to recognize it.
**Je vous en prie** is the polite form of "you're welcome". Its more casual relatives: *de rien*, and the most casual, *pas de problème*.
**En face de, à côté de, près de, loin de** all end in *de*, and that *de* merges with the article after it: *à côté **du** parc*, *en face **de la** gare*, *près **des** magasins*.
**Le quartier** is a very French word: not just a "neighborhood" but a little piece of the city with its own bakery, café and pharmacy. French daily life revolves around it.
**À dix minutes à pied** — notice that *à* is used for distance measured in travel time. *À cinq minutes en voiture*, *à une heure de Paris*.

grammars.title: Il y a and c'est
body: Both are often translated "there is" or "it is", but they do different jobs. *Il y a* introduces something's existence; *c'est* points it out and describes it.

head: Job
Form
Example
rows: *Il n'y a pas de banque ici.*

after: *Il y a* is also used for time gone by: *il y a deux ans* = two years ago. Context tells you which.
Asking how many: *Combien de chaises est-ce qu'il y a ?* or, more casually, *Il y a combien de chaises ?*

grammars.title: Saying where things are
body: The prepositions of place that cover almost every daily need. The ones ending in *de* merge with the article.
after: ⚠️ Merging *de* is compulsory, exactly like merging *à* in Unit 8: **de + le = du**, **de + les = des**. With *la* and *l'* nothing changes.
Writing *à côté de le parc* is a flat-out mistake. The correct form is *à côté du parc*.

grammars.title: à and de merging, the full picture
body: Two little rows that hold up hundreds of sentences. Learn them together.
after: A matching pair: *Je vais **au** marché et je reviens **du** marché.*

*Des* has two lives: the merged *de + les* (*je parle des enfants*) and the indefinite plural article (*j'ai des amis*). Same form, and context tells them apart — so don't be confused when you find it in two different places.

blocks.title: Lifesaver phrases
items: *Il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?* — Is there a pharmacy near here?
*C'est loin ?* — Is it far?
*C'est à combien de minutes à pied ?* — How many minutes on foot?
*Où sont les toilettes ?* — Where are the restrooms?
*Est-ce que c'est ouvert le dimanche ?* — Is it open on Sundays?
